parole.significato: Used to form verbs from nouns or adjectives, especially similative verbs
parole.testo: From Middle English -isen, from Middle French -iser, from Late Latin -izāre, from Ancient Greek -ίζω (-ízō), from Proto-Indo-European *-idyé- (verbal suffix). Cognate with Old English -ettan (verbal suffix).

parole.significato: Belonging to, relating to, or pertaining to an abbey, abbot, or abbess.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English abbacyal, derived from Middle French abbatial, derived from Late Latin abbātiāl|is, ~e, from abbā|s, ~tis (“abbot”) + -āl|is, ~e (“-ial”). Doublet of abbot.

parole.significato: An abominable act; a disgusting vice; a despicable habit.
parole.testo: From Middle English abominacioun, from Middle French abomination (“horror, disgust”), from Late Latin abōminātiō, abōminātiōnem (“abomination”) Doublet of abominatio.

parole.significato: The meaning (sense) in which a word or expression is understood, or generally received.
parole.testo: From Middle English acceptacioun, acceptation, from Middle French acceptacion and Late Latin acceptātiō. By surface analysis, accept + -ation.

parole.significato: A poem or other text in which certain letters, often the first in each line, spell out a name or message.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French acrostiche, acrostique (“acrostic”) (modern French acrostiche), and its etymon Late Latin acrostichis, from Ancient Greek ἀκροστιχίς (akrostikhís), from ἄκρο- (ákro-, prefix indicating, among other things, the extremity or tip of something) + στῐ́χος (stĭ́khos, “row or fi

parole.significato: Any of several perennial herbaceous plants, of the genus Agrimonia, that have spikes of yellow flowers.
parole.testo: From Middle English egremoyne, from a conflation of Old English agrimonia and Middle French agremoine (from Old French agremoine, variant of aegremone), both from Late Latin agrimōnia, metathesized from Latin argemōnia (“a kind of poppy”) (probably by association with ager, agri- (“field”)), from An

parole.significato: An acute fever.
parole.testo: From Middle English agu, ague, borrowed from Middle French (fievre) aguë, “acute (fever)” (Modern French fièvre aiguë), from Late Latin (febris) acuta (“acute fever”), from Latin acūtus (“sharp, acute”) + febris (“fever”). Doublet of acute.

parole.significato: The state of being previous or preceding in time or in situation.
parole.testo: From Middle French antériorité, from Late Latin anteriōritās, corresponding to anterior + -ity.

parole.significato: To divide and distribute portions of a whole.
parole.testo: From Middle French apportionner, from Old French aporcioner, from Late Latin apportionare, from Latin ad + portio. By surface analysis, ap- + portion.

parole.significato: Fragrant or spicy.
parole.testo: Late Middle English, from Middle French and Old French aromatique, from Late Latin aromaticus, from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).

parole.significato: Causing attraction; having the quality of attracting by inherent force.
parole.testo: From Middle French attractif, from Late Latin attractīvus, equivalent to attract + -ive.

parole.significato: Able to be heard.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French audible, from Late Latin audibilis, from Latin audire (“to hear”).

parole.significato: To increase; to make larger or supplement.
parole.testo: From Middle English augmenten, from Middle French augmenter, from Old French augmenter, from Late Latin augmentare (“to increase”), from Latin augmentum (“an increase, growth”), from augere (“to increase”).

parole.significato: A formal dance.
parole.testo: From Middle French bal, from Middle French baler (“to dance”), from Old French baller, from Late Latin ballō (“to dance”). Doublet of baile.

parole.significato: A small sailing vessel, e.g. a pinnace or a fishing smack; a rowing boat or barge.
parole.testo: From Middle English barke (“boat”), from Middle French barque, from Late Latin barca, a regular syncope of Vulgar Latin *barica, from Classical Latin bāris, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris, “Egyptian boat”), from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare, “small boat”), from Demotic Egyptian br, from Egyptian bꜣjrb-bA-A-

parole.significato: A sailing vessel of three or more masts, with all masts but the sternmost square-rigged, the sternmost being fore-and-a…
parole.testo: From Middle English barke (“boat”), borrowed from Middle French barque, itself borrowed from Italian barca or a Medieval Latin equivalent, from Late Latin barca, from Vulgar Latin barica, from Ancient Greek βᾶρις (bâris) 'Egyptian boat', from Coptic ⲃⲁⲁⲣⲉ (baare, “small boat”), from Demotic Egyptian

parole.significato: A twilled or corded fabric made from silk, wool, or cotton dyed black.
parole.testo: From Middle French bombasin, from Late Latin bombasinum, ultimately from bombyx (“silkworm”).

parole.significato: A machine, used for the purpose of giving cloth, paper etc., a smooth, even, and glossy or glazed surface, by cold or h…
parole.testo: * From Middle French calandre, from Late Latin calendra, altered from Latin cylindrus (“cylinder”), from Ancient Greek κύλινδρος (kúlindros). Doublet of calander and cylinder. * This spelling calender was introduced in the 17th century to differentiate the machine from the chronological senses of ca

parole.significato: Able and efficient; having the ability needed for a specific task; having the disposition to do something; permitting o…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French capable, from Late Latin capābilis.

parole.significato: Happening by chance.
parole.testo: From Middle French casuel, from Late Latin cāsuālis (“happening by chance”), from Latin cāsus (“event”) (English case), from cadere (“to fall”) (whence English cadence).

parole.significato: To burn and hence seal open tissue using a heated article or caustic agent so as to stop bleeding or minimise the risk…
parole.testo: From Middle French cauteriser, from Late Latin cauterizō (“to burn with a hot iron”), from Ancient Greek καυτηριάζω (kautēriázō, “to brand”), from καυτήρ (kautḗr, “branding iron”), from καίω (kaíō, “to burn”).

parole.significato: A hole or hollow depression in a solid object.
parole.testo: From Middle French cavité or Late Latin cavitās, from cav(i) (“hollow, excavated, concave”) + -tās (“-ity”, nominal suffix). First attested in the Mid-16th c.

parole.significato: Sureness, certainty.
parole.testo: From Middle French certitude, from Late Latin certitūdō, from Latin certus.

parole.significato: Chamois-colored.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French chamois, from Late Latin camox, from Gaulish camox (5th c. AD, Polemius Silvius), probably from an extinct Alpine language (Raetic, Ancient Ligurian), possibly Proto-Indo-European *kem- (“without horns”). Compare also Old High German gamiza (“chamois”) (whence modern Germ

parole.significato: A map.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French charte (“card, map”), from Late Latin charta (“paper, card, map”), Latin charta (“papyrus, writing”), from Ancient Greek χάρτης (khártēs, “papyrus, thin sheet”). Doublet of card and carte; related to charter.

parole.significato: To bring (two or more things or activities) together; to unite.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle English combynyn, from Middle French combiner, from Late Latin combīnāre (“unite, yoke together”), from Latin con- (“together”) + bīnī (“two by two”).

parole.significato: Suitable to be eaten; edible.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French comestible, or its source, Late Latin comestibilis, from Latin comedō (“to eat”), from com- (English com-) + edō (“I eat”) (as in English edible), from Proto-Indo-European (whence also English eat). Cognate with Spanish comestible (“grocery”). Attested as adjective in lat

parole.significato: The quality or state of being competent, i.e. able or suitable for a general role.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compétence, from Late Latin competentia. Doublet of competency.

parole.significato: Broadly or completely covering; including a large proportion of something.
parole.testo: Borrowed from late Middle French compréhensif, from Late Latin comprehēnsīvus, from Latin comprehendō.

parole.significato: A multiply folded piece of cloth, a pouch of ice, etc., used to apply to a patient's skin, cover the dressing of wounds…
parole.testo: From Middle French compresse, from compresse (“to compress”), from Late Latin compressare (“to press hard/together”), from Latin compressus, the past participle of comprimō (“to compress”), itself from com- (“together”) + premō (“press”).

parole.significato: An irrational need or irresistible urge to perform some action, often despite negative consequences.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French compulsion, from Late Latin compulsiō, from Latin compellere (“to compel, coerce”); see compel.

parole.significato: Opposition or contrariness; cross-purposes, marked contrast.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French contrariété, from Late Latin contrarietas, from contrarius, from Latin contra (“against”). By surface analysis, contrary + -ety.

parole.significato: A gradual healing after illness or injury.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French convalescence, from Late Latin convalēscentia (“regaining of health”), from Latin convalēscēn(t-)s, present participle of convalēscere (“to become strong or well”); see convalesce.

parole.significato: The act of coordinating, making different people or things work together for a goal or effect.
parole.testo: From Middle French coordination, from Late Latin coōrdinātiōnem (accusative of coōrdinātiō), from con- + ōrdinātiō. Morphologically coordinate + -ion.

parole.significato: Synonym of copiousness.
parole.testo: From Middle French copiosité or Late Latin cōpiōsitās. By surface analysis, copi(ous) + -osity.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a decree.
parole.testo: From Middle French decretal, from Late Latin dēcrētālis, from Latin decretum.

parole.significato: Tenfold.
parole.testo: From Middle English decuple, from Middle French décuple, from Late Latin decuplus (“tenfold”), from Latin decem (“ten”), and plicō (“fold”).

parole.significato: The act of deputing, or of appointing or commissioning a deputy or representative; office of a deputy or delegate; vice…
parole.testo: From Middle French députation, from Late Latin deputatio.

parole.significato: The state or process of being desiccated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dessiccation, from Late Latin desiccatio, desiccationem, from Latin desicco.

parole.significato: Of, being, or pertaining to a devil or the Devil.
parole.testo: From Middle English diabolik, from Middle French diabolique, from Late Latin diabolicus, from Ancient Greek διαβολικός (diabolikós, “devilish”), from διάβολος (diábolos, “devil”). First attested in 1350–1400.

parole.significato: A gastrointestinal disorder characterized by frequent and very soft or watery bowel movements.
parole.testo: From Middle English diaria, from Middle French diarrie (French diarrhée), from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”). By surface analysis, dia- + -rrhea. Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and

parole.significato: Dated spelling of diarrhoea.
parole.testo: From Middle French diarrie (French diarrhée), from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “flow”). Spelling later altered to resemble the word's Latin and Greek roots.

parole.significato: One who directs; the person in charge of managing a department or directorate (e.g., director of engineering), project,…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French directeur and its source Late Latin dīrēctōrem, from Latin dīrēctus. By surface analysis, direct + -or.

parole.significato: Adhering only to principles which are true a priori, rather than truths based on evidence or deduction.
parole.testo: From Middle French dogmatique and its etymon, Late Latin dogmaticus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós, “didactic”), from δόγμα (dógma, “dogma”).

parole.significato: A measured portion of medicine taken at any one time.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dose, from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), used by Galen and other Greek physicians to mean an amount of medicine, from δίδωμι (dídōmi, “to give”). Mostly displaced English drench. Doublet of doos.

parole.significato: The act of duplicating.
parole.testo: From Middle English duplicacioun, from Middle French duplication, from Late Latin duplicātiō, duplicātiōnem, from Latin duplicō. Morphologically duplicate + -ion.

parole.significato: A series of rulers or dynasts from one family.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French dynastie, from Late Latin dynastia, from Ancient Greek δυναστεία (dunasteía, “power, dominion”).

parole.significato: To give self-confidence to.
parole.testo: From Middle French effronter, from Old French esfronter, from Late Latin effrontō, from the prefix ex- (“from”) + frōns (“forehead”).

parole.significato: The impetus behind all motion and all activity.
parole.testo: From Middle French énergie, from Late Latin energia, from Ancient Greek ἐνέργεια (enérgeia, “activity”), from ἐνεργός (energós, “active”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + ἔργον (érgon, “work”). The sense in physics was coined by English polymath Thomas Young in 1802 in his lectures on Natural Philosophy.

parole.significato: An intensity of feeling; an excited interest or eagerness.
parole.testo: First attested from 1603, from Middle French enthousiasme, from Late Latin enthusiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”) + οὐσία (ousía, “essence”).

parole.significato: Occupying a position midway between two ends or sides.
parole.testo: From Middle French équidistant, from Late Latin aequidistantem, from aequī (“equal”) + distantem (“distant”). By surface analysis, equi- + distant.

parole.significato: A superficial structure of dead tissue, usually hardened, and commonly but not necessarily dark, adhering to underlying…
parole.testo: From Middle French eschare (now escarre) or Late Latin eschara (“scar, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “hearth, brazier, scab”). Doublet of scar.

parole.significato: Morality.
parole.testo: From Middle English etik, from Middle French ethique, from Late Latin ethica, from Ancient Greek ἠθική (ēthikḗ), from ἠθικός (ēthikós, “of or for morals, moral, expressing character”), from ἦθος (êthos, “character, moral nature”).

parole.significato: The act of eluding or evading or avoiding, particularly the pressure of an argument, accusation, charge, or interrogati…
parole.testo: From Middle French évasion, from Late Latin evasionem (accusative of evasio).

parole.significato: The act of evicting.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French éviction, from Late Latin ēvictiō, from Latin ēvincō.

parole.significato: The process of removing or ejecting material that has no further utility, especially from the body; the act of excretin…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French excrétion, or Late Latin excretio, excretionis, from Latin excerno.

parole.significato: The demands or requirements of a situation which often demand immediate action.
parole.testo: From Middle French exigence, from Late Latin exigentia (“urgency”) (from exigēns + -ia), from exigere (“to demand”).

parole.significato: That may be exacted; demandable; requirable.
parole.testo: From Middle French exigible, from Late Latin exigibilis, from exigō (“exact, execute”) + -ibilis.

parole.significato: The quality of being meagre or scanty.
parole.testo: From Middle French exiguite, from Late Latin exiguitas. See exiguous.

parole.significato: The action of expressing thoughts, ideas, feelings, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French expression, from Late Latin expressiō, expressiōnem (“a pressing out”). Morphologically express + -ion.

parole.significato: Something that is false; an untrue assertion.
parole.testo: Corresponding to false + -ity. From Middle French fausseté, Old French falseté, from Late Latin falsitas, from Latin falsus.

parole.significato: Wonderful; marvelous; excellent; extraordinarily good or great (used especially as an intensifier).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fantastique, borrowed from Late Latin phantasticus, borrowed from Ancient Greek φᾰντᾰστῐκός (phăntăstĭkós, “imaginary, fantastic; fictional”), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *bʰeh₂- (“to shine”). Equivalent to fantasy + -tic. Doublet of fantastique.

parole.significato: The derivative of a function.
parole.testo: From Middle French fluxion, from Late Latin fluxiō, from Latin flūxus + -iō.

parole.significato: The act of fortifying; the art or science of fortifying places to strengthen defence against an enemy.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French fortification, from Late Latin fortificatio, fortificationem, from fortifico, from Latin fortis. By surface analysis, fort + -ification.

parole.significato: To shiver or shudder.
parole.testo: From Middle English fremyssh, *fremysshen, from (the stem of) Middle French fremir, from Late Latin *fremīre, from Latin fremere.

parole.significato: furiousness; fury
parole.testo: From Middle English furiosite, from Middle French furiosité or its etymon Late Latin furiōsitās, from Latin furiōsus + -itās.

parole.significato: Any rent, charge, tribute, custom, tax, duty, excise etc.
parole.testo: A form of gavel (“rent, tax”) influenced by Middle French gabelle, from Late Latin gabella, gabulum, gablum; of uncertain origin. Compare gavel (“tribute”).

parole.significato: The leg or shank, typically of an animal, especially of a lion, on a coat of arms, crest, etc.
parole.testo: From Middle French gambe (variant of jambe) from Late Latin gamba (hoof, leg, shank). Doublet of jamb, gamba, and gam.

parole.significato: An element (individual sign or glyph) of a hieroglyphic writing system.
parole.testo: First attested around 1598, a back-formation from hieroglyphic (1580s), from Middle French hiéroglyphique, from Late Latin hieroglyphicus, from Ancient Greek ἱερογλυφικός (hierogluphikós) (Plutarch τά ἱερογλυφικά [γράμματα] "hieroglyphic [writing]), ἱερόγλυφος (hierógluphos, “carver of hieroglyphs”)

parole.significato: The act of humiliating or humbling someone; abasement of pride; mortification.
parole.testo: From Middle French humiliation, from Late Latin humiliātiō, from humiliāre (“to humiliate”); see humiliate. Equivalent to humiliate + -ion.

parole.significato: A membrane which completely or partially occludes the vaginal opening in human females.
parole.testo: From Middle French hymen, from Late Latin hymēn, from Ancient Greek ὑμήν (humḗn, “skin; membrane”).

parole.significato: A tentative conjecture explaining an observation, phenomenon or scientific problem and that can be tested by further ob…
parole.testo: Recorded since 1596, from Middle French hypothese, from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument, supposition”, literally “a placing under”), itself from ὑποτίθημι (hupotíthēmi, “to set before, suggest”), from ὑπό (hupó, “below”) + τίθημι (títhēmi,

parole.significato: Consisting of iambs (metrical feet with an unstressed–stressed pattern) or characterized by their predominance.
parole.testo: From Middle French iambique, from Late Latin ïambicus, from Ancient Greek ἰαμβικός (iambikós), from ἴαμβος (íambos) + -ικός (-ikós).

parole.significato: Sameness, identicalness; the quality or fact of (several specified things) being the same.
parole.testo: From Middle English ydemptite, from Middle French identité and its etymon Late Latin idemptitās, identitās, from idem (“the same”) + -tās (suffix forming abstract nouns) as a calque of Ancient Greek ταὐτότης (tautótēs, “sameness”).

parole.significato: A manner of speaking, a mode of expression peculiar to a language, language family, or group of people.
parole.testo: From Middle French idiome, and its source, Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “a peculiarity, property, a peculiar phraseology, idiom”), from ἰδιοῦσθαι (idioûsthai, “to make one's own, appropriate to oneself”), from ἴδιος (ídios, “one's own, pertaining to oneself, private, persona

parole.significato: The act of illuminating, or supplying with light; the state of being illuminated.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French illumination, from Late Latin illūminātiō, from Latin illumino. Equivalent to illuminate + -ion.

parole.significato: To give or bestow (e.g. a quality or property).
parole.testo: From Middle English imparten, borrowed from Middle French impartir, empartir, from Late Latin impartiō, impertiō, from im- (“in”) + Latin partiō (“divide”).

parole.significato: The act or conduct of an impostor; deception practiced under a false or assumed character; fraud or imposition.
parole.testo: From Middle French imposture, from Late Latin impostura, Latin impostus.

parole.significato: Not able to be accessed; out of reach; inconvenient.
parole.testo: From Middle French inaccessible, from Late Latin inaccessibilis, equivalent to in- + accessible. Piecewise doublet of unaccessible.

parole.significato: A cut, especially one made by a scalpel or similar medical tool in the context of surgical operation; the scar resultin…
parole.testo: From Middle English inscicioun, from Middle French incision, from Late Latin incisiō from the verb incidō (“to cut into”) + action noun suffix -iō.

parole.significato: The state of being uncivil; lack of courtesy; rudeness in manner.
parole.testo: From Middle French incivilité, from Late Latin incivilitas (“incivility”), from Latin incivilis (“impolite, uncivil”), from in- (privative prefix) + civilis (“belonging to a citizen, civic, political, urbane, courteous, civil”) (from civis (“a citizen”)), equivalent to in- + civility.

parole.significato: Security from damage, loss, or penalty.
parole.testo: From late Middle English indempnite, from Middle French indemnité, from Late Latin indemnitās (“security from damage”), from Latin indemnis (“undamaged”), from in- (“not”) + damnum (“damage”).

parole.significato: That is incapable of being measured.
parole.testo: From Middle French indeterminable, from Late Latin indeterminabilis.

parole.significato: Serving as a sign, indication or suggestion of something.
parole.testo: From Middle French indicatif, from Late Latin indicātīvus. By surface analysis, indicate + -ive.

parole.significato: The state of being indifferent.
parole.testo: From Middle French indifférence, from Late Latin indifferentia. By surface analysis, in- + difference.

parole.significato: Not direct
parole.testo: From Middle French indirect, from Late Latin indirectus (“not direct”).

parole.significato: Incapable of being divided; atomic.
parole.testo: PIE word  *dwóh₁ From Middle French indivisible, from Late Latin indivisibilis. Equivalent to in- + divisible.

parole.significato: Of, or relating to logical induction, by generalizing a universal claim or principle from the observed particular insta…
parole.testo: From Middle French inductif, from Late Latin inductivus.

parole.significato: Hard-working and persistent.
parole.testo: From Middle French industrieux, from Late Latin industriosus (“diligent, active, industrious”), from Latin industria (“diligence, industry”); see industry.

parole.significato: The state or quality of being inelegant; lack of grace, refinement, beauty, or polish in language, composition, or mann…
parole.testo: From Middle French inélégance, from Late Latin inelegantia.

parole.significato: Not fertile.
parole.testo: From Middle French infertile, from Late Latin infertilis, equivalent to in- + fertile.

parole.significato: The condition of being infertile; of having poor fertility.
parole.testo: From Middle French infertilité, from Late Latin infertilitas.

parole.significato: The presence of a large number of pest organisms in an area or field, on the surface of a host or anything that might c…
parole.testo: From Middle French infestation, from Late Latin infestatio. Morphologically infest + -ation.

parole.significato: One who infracts or infringes; a violator; a rule breaker.
parole.testo: Probably from Middle French infracteur, from Late Latin īnfrāctor.

parole.significato: The act of innovating; the introduction of something new, in customs, rites, etc.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French innovation, from Old French innovacion, from Late Latin innovatio, innovationem, from Latin innovo, innovatus. Morphologically innovate + -ion.

parole.significato: Not satiable; incapable of being satisfied or appeased; very greedy.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English insaciable, from Middle French insatiable, from Old French insaciable, from Late Latin insatiabilis. By surface analysis, in- + satiable.

parole.significato: That cannot be tolerated or endured.
parole.testo: From Middle French insupportable, from Late Latin insupportabilis. See also in- + supportable.

parole.significato: Existing or occurring without interruption or end; ceaseless, unending.
parole.testo: From Middle English interminable, from Middle French interminable and its etymon Late Latin interminābilis. By surface analysis, in- + terminable.

parole.significato: A military action consisting of a large armed force of one geopolitical entity entering territory controlled by another…
parole.testo: From Middle French invasion, from Late Latin invāsiōnem, accusative of invāsiō.

parole.significato: Unable to be reconciled; opposed; uncompromising.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French irréconciliable, from Late Latin irreconciliābilis, from in- (“not”) + reconciliō (“to reconcile”) + -ābilis (“-able”). By surface analysis, ir- + reconcilable.

parole.significato: The state of being jocund.
parole.testo: From Middle English jocundite, from Middle French jocundité, from Late Latin iōcunditās. By surface analysis, jocund + -ity. Doublet of jucundity.

parole.significato: A special year of emancipation supposed to be observed every fifty years, when farming was temporarily stopped, certain…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English jubile [and other forms], from Middle French jubile, from Old French jubilee, jubileus (modern French jubilé), from Late Latin iūbilaeus (adjective, also treated as a noun), from Ancient Greek ἰωβηλαῖος (iōbēlaîos, “of a jubilee”), from ἰώβηλος (iṓbēlos, “jubilee”) + -ῐος (-

parole.significato: A reason, explanation, or excuse which someone believes provides convincing, morally acceptable support for behavior or…
parole.testo: From Middle English justificacioun, justification, from Middle French justification, from Late Latin iustificationem, justificationem < iustificatio, from iustifico, from Latin iustus.

parole.significato: Light; slender, slim; trivial.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French legier, from Old French legier, apparently from Late Latin *leviārium, from levis (“light in weight”). See levity.

parole.significato: The act of tying or binding something.
parole.testo: From Middle English ligature, from Middle French ligature, from Late Latin ligātūra, from ligāre (“to tie, bind”).

parole.significato: A dull, stupid fellow; a lout.
parole.testo: Likely from Middle French lourdin (“dull, obvious; clownish”) (related to lourdat (“dunce”), lourdade (“wench”)), from Middle French lourd (“heavy”), from Old French lourt, from Late Latin lurdus, possibly of Germanic origin. Cognate with Dutch loerd, French lourdant, Scottish Gaelic lurdan, this la

parole.significato: Dissatisfied with current conditions; disaffected, discontented, rebellious.
parole.testo: From Middle French malcontent, from mal- + content; compare Late Latin malecontentus.

parole.significato: Harmful, malevolent, injurious.
parole.testo: From Middle French malignant, from Late Latin malignans. See malign.

parole.significato: Able to be hammered into thin sheets; capable of being extended or shaped by beating with a hammer, or by the pressure…
parole.testo: From Middle French malléable, borrowed from Late Latin malleābilis, derived from Latin malleāre (“to hammer”), from malleus (“hammer”), from Proto-Indo-European *mal-ni- (“crushing”), an extended variant of *melh₂- (“crush, grind”).

parole.significato: Resembling a breast or nipple in shape or form.
parole.testo: From Middle French mamillaire or directly from Late Latin mammillāris, from mamilla + -aris, diminutive of mamma (“breast”).

parole.significato: Synonym of matutinal.
parole.testo: A variant of matutinal (possibly influenced by French matin (“morning”)), which is borrowed from Middle French matutinal (modern French matutinal), and from its etymon Late Latin mātūtīnālis (“(adjective) belonging to the morning; of or pertaining to matins; (noun) morning hymn or psalm; book of lau

parole.significato: Of, occurring in, or relating to the morning, especially the early morning upon waking up.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French matutinal (modern French matutinal), and from its etymon Late Latin mātūtīnālis (“(adjective) belonging to the morning; of or pertaining to matins; (noun) morning hymn or psalm; book of lauds”), from Latin mātūtīnus (“of, occurring in, or pertaining to the early morning,

parole.significato: Negotiation to resolve differences conducted by an impartial party.
parole.testo: From Middle English mediacion, mediacioun, medyacion, medyacyoun from Middle French mediacion and its etymon Late Latin mediātiō, from mediārī (“intervene”), from Latin medius (“middle”). By surface analysis, mediate + -ion.

parole.significato: A headache; a migraine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French migraigne, semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin hēmicrānia (“pain in one half of the head”), from Ancient Greek ἡμικρᾱνίᾰ (hēmikrāníă), from ἡμι- (hēmi-, “hemi-, half”) + κρανίον (kraníon, “skull”) (whence also English cranium). Doublet of migraine and hemicrania.

parole.significato: Of or relating to the mind or specifically the total emotional and intellectual response of an individual to external r…
parole.testo: Borrowing from Middle French mental, from Late Latin mentālis, from mēns (“mind, disposition; heart, soul”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix).

parole.significato: The practice of judging someone's character, or telling their fortune, from studying their face or forehead.
parole.testo: From Middle French metoposcopie, and its source, Late Latin metoposcopia, ultimately from Ancient Greek μέτωπον (métōpon, “forehead”) + -scopy.

parole.significato: Threatening, menacing.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French minatoire, from Late Latin minātōrius. Compare menace.

parole.significato: The state or condition of being smaller, inferior, or subordinate to something or someone else; lesserness.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English minoritie, from Middle French minorité, and its source Late Latin minōritās, from Latin minor. Morphologically minor + -ity.

parole.significato: Pertaining to a current or recent time and style; not ancient.
parole.testo: From Middle French moderne, from Late Latin modernus; from Latin modo (“just now”), originally ablative of modus (“measure”); hence, by measure, "just now". See also mode.

parole.significato: A half.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French moytié, from Old French meitié (“half”) (modern French moitié (“half”)), from Late Latin medietās (“centre, midpoint; half”), from Latin medius (“half; middle”) + -tās (from Proto-Indo-European *-teh₂ts (suffix forming nouns indicating a state of being)). Medius is ultima

parole.significato: Momentary, transient.
parole.testo: From Middle French momentané, from Late Latin momentaneus.

parole.significato: The ruler of an absolute monarchy or the head of state of a constitutional monarchy.
parole.testo: From Middle French monarque, from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”), from μόνος (mónos, “only”) + ἀρχός (arkhós, “leader”), equivalent to mono- + -arch. * (butterfly): See monarch butterfly.

parole.significato: Of or relating to monasteries or monks.
parole.testo: From Middle French monastique, from Late Latin monasticus.

parole.significato: Of, pertaining to, or consisting of money.
parole.testo: From Middle French monétaire, from Late Latin monētārius (“pertaining to money”), from Latin monētārius (“of a mint”), from monēta (“mint, coinage”), from the presence—from 273 BC to AD 84—of the chief Roman mint at the Templum Iunonis Monetae (“Temple of Juno Moneta”), q.v. Doublet of minter.

parole.significato: An appellation owned by a single winery.
parole.testo: From the Middle French monopole or its etymon the Late Latin monopōlium (“a monopoly”).

parole.significato: An organism showing abnormal development or deformity.
parole.testo: From Middle English monstruosite, from Middle French monstruosité and its etymon Late Latin mōnstruōsitās, mōnstrōsitās (“monstrousness”), from Latin mōnstruōsus, mōnstrōsus; by surface analysis, monstrous + -ity.

parole.significato: Having many mountains; characterized by mountains; of the nature of a mountain; rough (terrain); rocky.
parole.testo: From mountain + -ous after Middle French montagneux, from Late Latin montāniōsus, from montānia, from Latin montem (“mountain”).

parole.significato: A thick gluey substance (gum) produced by many plants and some microorganisms.
parole.testo: From Middle English muscilage, mussillage, from Middle French mucilage (“viscous substance found in vegetable material”), from Late Latin mūcilāgō (“musty or moldy juice”). See Greek μούχλα (moúchla, “mold”), and related derivatives, for example mushroom, from *meus- (“mosses, mold, mildew”).

parole.significato: wall
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English muren, from Middle French murer, from Old French murer (“to close by a wall”), from Late Latin mūrō, mūrāre, from Latin mūrus (“wall”). Related to German Mauer (“wall”).

parole.significato: Any of various small bagpipes having a soft sound, especially with a bellows, which were popular in France in the 17th…
parole.testo: From both of the following: * Late Middle English musette (“type of bagpipe”), from Middle French musette, Old French musette (“type of bagpipe”) (modern French musette), from muse (“bagpipe”) + -ette (diminutive suffix). Muse is derived from muser (“to play the bagpipe; (figuratively) to flatter”),

parole.significato: Shaped like a boat.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French naviculaire, itself borrowed from Late Latin nāviculāris (“boat shaped”), from Latin nāvicula, diminutive of nāvis (“ship”), from Proto-Indo-European *néh₂us.

parole.significato: Unequalled, unrivalled; unique.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English non-parail (“unparalleled, nonpareil”) [and other forms], from Middle French nonpareille, nonpareil (“unparalleled”) (obsolete), from non- (prefix meaning ‘not’) + pareil (“alike, like, same”). Pareil is derived from Old French pareil, from Late Latin pāriculus (“equal; like

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to nutrition.
parole.testo: From Middle French nutritif, from Late Latin nūtritīvus, from the participle stem of Latin nūtriō (“to suckle”).

parole.significato: Abusive language.
parole.testo: From Middle English obloqui, obloquie, obloquy, from Middle French obloquie and its etymon Late Latin obloquium (“contradiction”), from Latin obloquor (“speak against, contradict”). By surface analysis, ob- + -loquy.

parole.significato: A short poetical composition proper to be set to music or sung; a lyric poem; especially, now, a poem characterized by…
parole.testo: From Middle French ode, from Late Latin ōda, from Ancient Greek ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”). Doublet of Aoede.

parole.significato: Conjectural; expressing an opinion rather than a fact.
parole.testo: From opine + -ate + -ive. Middle French opinatif, and its source, Late Latin opinativus, from the participle stem of Latin opīnārī.

parole.significato: Causing opprobrium; offensive and shameful.
parole.testo: From Middle English opprobrious, from Middle French opprobrieux and its etymon Late Latin opprobriōsus.

parole.significato: Expressing a wish or a choice.
parole.testo: From Middle French optatif, from Late Latin optātīvus, a calque of Ancient Greek εὐκτική (euktikḗ, “related to wishing”), from Latin optātus, past participle of optāre.

parole.significato: A mouth or aperture, such as of a tube, pipe, etc.; an opening.
parole.testo: From Middle French, from Old French, from Late Latin ōrificium (“an opening, literally the making of a mouth”), compound of ōs (“mouth”) + faciō (“to make”).

parole.significato: Conforming to the accepted, established, or traditional doctrines of a given faith, religion, or ideology.
parole.testo: From Late Middle English orthodoxe, from Middle French orthodoxe and its etymon Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos), from ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) + δόξα (dóxa, “opinion”). Displaced native Old English wuldorlīċ.

parole.significato: Apparently true, but not necessarily; ostensible
parole.testo: From Middle French ostensif and its etymon Late Latin ostēnsīvus.

parole.significato: Rebirth; regeneration.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French, French palingénésie, from Late Latin palingenesia: see further at palingenesis.

parole.significato: A membrane of tissue in the body of a human or animal.
parole.testo: From Middle French pannicle, and its source, Late Latin panniculus (“membrane”), from Latin panniculus (“small rag”), from pannus (“cloth”).

parole.significato: A fallacious argument or illogical conclusion, especially one committed by mistake, or believed by the speaker to be lo…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French paralogisme, from Late Latin paralogismus, from Ancient Greek παραλογισμός (paralogismós).

parole.significato: Equality; comparability of strength or intensity.
parole.testo: From Middle French parité, from Late Latin paritās, from Latin pār (“equal”). Equivalent to pari- + -ty.

parole.significato: Parley; talk.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English parlen (“to speak”), from Middle French parler, from Old French parler, from Late Latin parabolō.

parole.significato: A period (especially one of several recurring periods) during the course of an illness when symptoms worsen; a sudden a…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English paroxism, paroxisme (“period of worsening of a disease, attack; sudden recurrent fever”), from Middle French paroxisme, paroxysme, and Old French peroxime (“period of worsening of a disease; bout of fever or illness”) (modern French paroxysme), and from their etymon Late Lat

parole.significato: The act of participating, of taking part in something.
parole.testo: From Middle English participacioun, from Middle French [Term?], from Old French participacion, from Late Latin participatiō. By surface analysis, participate + -ion.

parole.significato: A particular thing.
parole.testo: From Middle French particularité (“part of a whole; something particular, particularity”) (modern French particularité), and from its etymon Late Latin particularitas (“fact or quality of being particular; something particular, particularity”), from Latin particulāris (“particular; partial”) + -tās

parole.significato: A person who loves and zealously supports and defends their country.
parole.testo: From Middle French patriote, from Late Latin patriōta (“fellow countryman”) from the Ancient Greek πατριώτης (patriṓtēs, “of the same country”), from πατρίς (patrís, “father land", "country”), from πατήρ (patḗr, “father”).

parole.significato: Of a person, etc.: that commits or has committed an offence or a sin; blameworthy, culpable, offending, sinful, sinning.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French peccant (“unhealthy”) (modern French peccant), and from its etymon Late Latin peccantis, the genitive singular of peccāns (“offending; sinning, transgressing”, adjective), from Latin peccāns (“wrongdoer”), a noun use of the active present participle of pe

parole.significato: To hang down; to cause something to hang down
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French pendre (“to hang”), from Late Latin pendĕre, from Latin pendēre.

parole.significato: A polygon with five sides and five angles.
parole.testo: From Middle French pentagone, from Late Latin pentagōnum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon), noun use of the neuter of the adjective πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”), from πέντε (pénte, “five”) + -γωνος (-gōnos, “angled”). Equivalent to penta- + -gon.

parole.significato: A bottle or other vessel for containing a liquid; originally any such vessel, especially one for holding a beverage; no…
parole.testo: The noun is derived partly: * from Middle English fiole, phiole, phial (“small bowl or cup for liquids, etc.; flask”) [and other forms], from Middle French fiole, phiole [and other forms], and Old French fiole (modern French fiole), from Late Latin fiola, phiola, from Latin phiala (“broad, flat, sha

parole.significato: A poem.
parole.testo: From Middle English poesie (Middle English po(esie) + -esy), from Middle French poesie, from Late Latin poesia, from earlier poēsis, from Ancient Greek ποίησις (poíēsis). Doublet of poiesis.

parole.significato: The pole star.
parole.testo: From pole + arctic, after Middle French pôle arctique, Late Latin polus arcticus.

parole.significato: The quality of being possible.
parole.testo: From Middle English possibilite, from Middle French possibilité (from Old French possibilite) and directly from Late Latin possibilitās (“possibility”), from Latin possibilis (“possible”); see possible. By surface analysis, possible + -ity.

parole.significato: Good for drinking without fear of waterborne disease or poisoning.
parole.testo: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English potable (“drinkable, potable”), from Middle French, Old French potable (modern French potable (“drinkable, potable”)), and from its etymon Late Latin pōtābilis (“drinkable, potable”), from Latin pōtāre (“to drink”) + -bilis (suffix forming adjectives

parole.significato: Practical, concerned with making decisions and actions that are useful in practice, not just theory.
parole.testo: From Middle French pragmatique, from Late Latin pragmaticus (“relating to civil affair; in Latin, as a noun, a person versed in the law who furnished arguments and points to advocates and orators, a kind of attorney”), from Ancient Greek πραγματικός (pragmatikós, “active, versed in affairs”), from π

parole.significato: A green gem; an emerald.
parole.testo: From Middle English [Term?], from a combination of Middle French prame (inherited from Late Latin prasinus) and Middle French prasine (borrowed from Late Latin prasinum), both ultimately from Latin prasinus (“leek-green”), from Ancient Greek πράσινος (prásinos), from πράσον (práson, “leek”).

parole.significato: Inclined to make rapid decisions without due consideration; hasty, impulsive, rash.
parole.testo: The adjective is borrowed from Middle French précipitant, Old French precipitant (“acting hastily, hasty, rash; acting, happening, or moving rapidly; pressing”) (modern French précipitant), and from their etymon Late Latin praecipitans (“hasty, rash”), an adjective use of Latin praecipitāns, the pre

parole.significato: The action of pretending; false or simulated show or appearance; false or hypocritical assertion or representation.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French pretensse, from Late Latin praetēnsus, past participle of Latin praetendō (“to pretend”), from prae- (“before”) + tendō (“to stretch”); see pretend.

parole.significato: Posing a problem; having or suffering from problem(s):
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French problématique, from Late Latin problematicus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”), from προβάλλω (probállō, “I throw, place before”), from πρό (pró, “before”) + βάλλω (bállō, “I throw, place”). By surf

parole.significato: Wastefully extravagant.
parole.testo: From Middle French prodigal, from Late Latin prōdigālis (“wasteful”), from Latin prōdigus (“wasteful, lavish, prodigal”), from prōdigō (“to consume, squander, drive forth”), from prōd- [from prō (“before, forward”)] + agō (“to drive”). Also see unrelated prodigy. The senses of "abandoning a person o

parole.significato: The act of profaning; desecration, blasphemous behaviour, defilement.
parole.testo: From Middle French prophanation, profanation, and its source, Late Latin profanatio, from the participle stem of Latin profānō. By surface analysis, profane + -ation.

parole.significato: abundance; the state of being profuse; a cornucopia
parole.testo: From Middle French profusion, from Late Latin profusio.

parole.significato: The act of prosecuting a scheme or endeavor.
parole.testo: Equivalent to prosecute + -ion, from Middle French prosecution, from Late Latin prōsecutio, from Latin prōsequor (“follow, pursue”), from pro- (“onward”) + sequor (“follow”) (English sequel). Compare persecution, and see more at prosecute.

parole.significato: A verse used in prosodia, having three anapests, of which the first may be substituted with a spondee or iamb.
parole.testo: From Middle French prosodiaque and its etymon Late Latin prosōdiacus, from Koine Greek προσοδιακός (prosodiakós), from Ancient Greek προσόδιον (prosódion) + -ακός (-akós). By surface analysis, prosodi(on) + -ac.

parole.significato: Likely or expected to happen or become.
parole.testo: From Middle French prospectif, from Late Latin prospectivus. See more at English prospect.

parole.significato: The minutes, or official record, of a negotiation or transaction; especially a document drawn up officially which forms…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French protocolle, protocole (“document, record”), from Late Latin protocollum (“the first sheet of a volume (on which contents and errata were written)”), from Byzantine Greek πρωτόκολλον (prōtókollon, “first sheet glued onto a manuscript”), from πρῶτος (prôtos, “first”) + κόλλ

parole.significato: Created first; archetypal.
parole.testo: From Middle French prothoplaste, and its source Late Latin protoplastus, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek πρωτόπλαστος (prōtóplastos, “first-formed”), from Ancient Greek πρωτο- (prōto-) + πλαστός (plastós, “formed, moulded”).

parole.significato: Serving or tending to elicit a strong, often negative sentiment in another person; exasperating.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French provocatif, and its source, Late Latin provocativus, from Latin provocare.

parole.significato: The study of the origins and development of the soul or mind.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French psychogonie, from Late Latin psychogonia, from Koine Greek ψυχογονία (psukhogonía), from ψυχή (psukhḗ, “soul, mind”) + γόνος (gónos, “descent”). By surface analysis, psycho- + -gony.

parole.significato: Synonym of quietness (“absence of sound”)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French quiétude, from Late Latin quiētūdō, from Latin quiētus, perfect passive participle of quiēscō (“rest”).

parole.significato: The wrist.
parole.testo: From Middle French rachette, rascette, from Late Latin racheta, rasceta (“wrist, ankle”), diminutive of rasca, from Arabic رَاحَة (rāḥa, “palm of the hand”).

parole.significato: Straightness; the state or quality of having a constant direction and not being crooked or bent.
parole.testo: From Middle English rectitude, from Middle French rectitude, from Late Latin rectitūdō (“straightness, uprightness”), from Latin rectus (“straight”), perfect passive participle of regō (“regulate, guide”).

parole.significato: Pertaining to the reduction of a decree etc.; rescissory.
parole.testo: From Middle French réductif, from Late Latin reductivus, from the participle stem of Latin reducere (“to reduce”).

parole.significato: The act of reflecting or the state of being reflected.
parole.testo: From Middle English refleccion, refleccioun, refleccioune, reflection, from Middle French reflection, reflexion, and its source Late Latin reflexiō, from the participle stem of reflectō. The current spelling is influenced by reflect. Equivalent to reflect + -ion.

parole.significato: Dated spelling of reflection.
parole.testo: From Middle English reflexion, reflexioun, from Middle French reflexion and its etymon Late Latin reflexiō; the variant spelling reflection is due to influence from correction.

parole.significato: A unit of armed troops under the command of an officer, and consisting of several smaller units.
parole.testo: From Middle French regement, régiment, and its source, Late Latin regimentum (“direction for government; course of medical treatment”), from Latin regō (“rule”).

parole.significato: The condition or quality of being regular
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French regularite, from Old French regularite, from Late Latin rēgulāritās, rēgulāritātem, from rēgulāris; see regular. By surface analysis, regular + -ity.

parole.significato: Connected to or depending on something else; comparative.
parole.testo: From Middle French relatif, from Late Latin relātīvus, from Latin relātus, perfect passive participle of referō (“to carry back, to ascribe”), from re- (“again”) + ferō (“to bear or carry”). By surface analysis, relate + -ive.

parole.significato: Something that, or someone who, survives or remains or is left over after the loss of others; a relic.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English relicte (“widow”), from Middle French relicte (“widow”), from Late Latin relicta (“widow”), from Latin relictus, past participle of relinquō (“to abandon, to relinquish, to leave (behind)”), from re- + linquō (“to leave, quit, forsake, depart from”). Doublet of relic, d

parole.significato: A container to hold or display religious relics.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French reliquaire (modern French reliquaire), from Late Latin reliquiarium, from rēliquia (“a relic”) (English relic), noun use of reliquus (“abandoned, left behind, relict”), from relinquō (“to relinquish”), from re- (“again”) and linquō (“to leave”), from Proto-Indo-European *

parole.significato: The act of sending an accused person back into custody whilst awaiting trial.
parole.testo: From Middle English remaunden (“to send back”), from Middle French remander (“to send back”), from Late Latin remandare (“to send backward”), from Latin remandare (“to order”). Compare countermand.

parole.significato: The act of repelling or the condition of being repelled.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French répulsion, from Late Latin repulsio, repulsionem, from Latin repulsus.

parole.significato: Answering, replying or responding
parole.testo: From Middle French responsif, from Late Latin responsivus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to laughter.
parole.testo: From Middle French risible and directly from Late Latin rīsibilis, from Latin rīsus (“laughter”) + -ibilis, from the perfect passive participle of rīdeō (“laugh”).

parole.significato: Bloody; containing blood.
parole.testo: From Middle English sanguinous, sangwynouse (“sanguine; of eyes: bloodshot”), from Middle French sanguineux and its etymon Late Latin sanguinōsus.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to satire.
parole.testo: From Middle French satirique, from Late Latin satiricus.

parole.significato: Done to satisfaction; adequate or sufficient.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French satisfactoire, from Late Latin satisfactōrius, from Latin satisfactus, past participle of satisfaciō.

parole.significato: A procedural plan, usually but not necessarily tabular in nature, indicating a sequence of operations and the planned t…
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English cedule, from Middle French cedule (whence French cédule), from Old French cedule, from Late Latin schedula (“papyrus strip”), diminutive of Latin scheda, from Ancient Greek σχέδη (skhédē, “papyrus leaf”), from Proto-Hellenic *skʰíd͏̌d͏̌ō, from Proto-Indo-European *skid-

parole.significato: Of, or relating to the ischium.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sciatique, from Late Latin sciaticus, variant of ischiadicus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).

parole.significato: Emotions or feelings arising from or relating to aesthetic or moral standards, especially those which are sensitive and…
parole.testo: From Late Middle English sensibilite (“physical ability to sense or perceive; sensitivity to pain; type of perception by a sense organ; perception, understanding; image imprinted on the mind during perception; (philosophy) capacity of the soul to receive information from the senses, perceptibility;

parole.significato: The state of being sensual or sensuous.
parole.testo: Derived from Middle French sensualité, derived from Late Latin sēnsuālitātem (“sensibility, capacity for sensation”). By surface analysis, sensual + -ity.

parole.significato: The process or act of sequestering; a putting aside or separating.
parole.testo: From Middle French sequestration, from Late Latin sequestrātiō, from Latin sequestrō (“sequester”).

parole.significato: A state of drowsiness or sleepiness.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French somnolence, from Late Latin somnolentia, derived from Latin somnus (“sleep”), from Proto-Indo-European *swépnos (“sleep, slumber”).

parole.significato: The quality or state of being spiritual.
parole.testo: From Middle French spiritualité, from Late Latin spīrituālitās.

parole.significato: The property of being stolid; unemotionality.
parole.testo: From stolid + -ity, from Middle French stolidité, from Late Latin stoliditas.

parole.significato: Of a lower rank or position; inferior or secondary; especially (military) ranking as a junior officer, below the rank o…
parole.testo: From Middle French subalterne, from Late Latin subalternus, from Latin sub- + alternus, from alter.

parole.significato: Real being; existence.
parole.testo: From Middle English subsistence; partly from Middle French subsistence (modern French subsistance) and partly from its etymon Late Latin subsistentia (“substance, reality, in Medieval Latin also stability”), from Latin subsistēns, present participle of subsistere (“to continue, subsist”). Perhaps al

parole.significato: The act of substituting or the state of being substituted.
parole.testo: From Middle French substitution, from Late Latin substitutio.

parole.significato: A subsidy; provision of financial or other support.
parole.testo: From Middle French subvention, from Late Latin subventio, from Latin subvenio (assist).

parole.significato: Superior to or notable above all others; outstanding; supremely remarkable.
parole.testo: From Middle French supereminent, and its source, Late Latin supereminens, adjectival use of Latin superēminēre (corresponding to super- + eminent).

parole.significato: Something written (or engraved) on the surface, outside, or above something else; specifically, an address on a letter,…
parole.testo: From Middle French superscription, or its source, Late Latin superscriptio, from superscribere.

parole.significato: To encircle something or simultaneously extend in all directions.
parole.testo: From Middle English sourrounden (“to submerge, overflow”), from Middle French souronder, suronder, from Late Latin superundō, from super + undō (“to rise in waves”), from unda (“wave”).

parole.significato: A feeling of pity or sorrow for the suffering or distress of another.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French sympathie, from Late Latin sympathīa (“feeling in common”), from Ancient Greek σῠμπᾰ́θειᾰ (sŭmpắtheiă, “fellow feeling”), from σῠμπᾰθής (sŭmpăthḗs, “affected by like feelings; exerting mutual influence, interacting”) + -ῐᾰ (-ĭă, “-y”, nominal suffix). Equivalent to sym- (

parole.significato: A group or set of related things that operate together as a complex whole.
parole.testo: Partly borrowed from Middle French sisteme, systeme, partly directly from its etymon Late Latin systēma (“harmony; musical scale; set of celestial objects; set of troops; system”), from Ancient Greek σύστημα (sústēma, “musical scale; organized body; whole made of several parts or members”), from σῠν

parole.significato: Touchable; able to be touched or felt; perceptible by the sense of touch.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French tangible, from Late Latin tangibilis, from Latin tangere (“to touch”)

parole.significato: Of or situated in the temples of the head or the sides of the skull behind the orbits.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French timporal, temporal, from Late Latin temporālis, from tempora (“the temples of the head”) + -ālis (“-al”, adjectival suffix). Doublet of temporalis.

parole.significato: The quality of being terrible.
parole.testo: From Middle English terryblete, from Middle French terribleté, terribilité and its etymon, Late Latin terribilitās.

parole.significato: A mathematical statement of some importance that has been proven to be true. Minor theorems are often called propositio…
parole.testo: From Middle French théorème, from Late Latin theōrēma, from Ancient Greek θεώρημα (theṓrēma, “speculation, proposition to be proved”) (Euclid), from θεωρέω (theōréō, “to look at, view, consider, examine”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”), from θέα (théa, “a view”) + ὁράω (horáō, “to see, look”).

parole.significato: A description of an event or system that is considered to be accurate.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French théorie, a learned borrowing from Late Latin theōria, borrowed from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā).

parole.significato: The act, or an instance, of burning incense.
parole.testo: From Middle English, from Middle French thurification, from Late Latin thurificatio, from Latin thurificatus; equivalent to thus (“incense”) + -ification.

parole.significato: The act of turning or twisting, or the state of being twisted; the twisting or wrenching of a body by the exertion of a…
parole.testo: From Middle English torcion, from Middle French torsion, from Late Latin torsiōnem, from Latin tortiō, from torqueō (“twist, turn”). See torture, -tort.

parole.significato: The act of conducting or carrying out (business, negotiations, plans).
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French transaction, from Old French transaccion, from Late Latin transactio. By surface analysis, trans- + action.

parole.significato: A mason’s tool, used in spreading and dressing mortar, and breaking bricks to shape them.
parole.testo: From Middle English trowell, trouel, truel, from Middle French truelle, from Late Latin truella, from Classical Latin trulla, the diminutive of trua (“ladle”). Doublet of trullo.

parole.significato: Promoting the supremacy of the Pope.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French ultramontain, from Late Latin ultramontanus.

parole.significato: The condition of agreement by all parties, the state of being unanimous.
parole.testo: From unanim(ous) + -ity, from Middle French unanimité, from Late Latin ūnanimitās. Displaced native Old English ānmōdnes (literally “one-mindedness”).

parole.significato: Cause to become one; make into a unit; consolidate; merge; combine.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French unifier, from Late Latin unificare.

parole.significato: the property of being universal, common to all members of a class
parole.testo: From Middle English universalite, from Middle French universalité, from Old French, from Late Latin universalitas. By surface analysis, universal + -ity.

parole.significato: Synonym of urinary.
parole.testo: From Middle French urinal, from Late Latin ūrīnālis, equivalent to urine + -al.

parole.significato: A usurper.
parole.testo: From Middle French usurpateur or Late Latin ūsūrpātor.

parole.significato: The state of being valid, authentic or genuine.
parole.testo: From valid + -ity, borrowed from Middle French validité, from Late Latin validitas.

parole.significato: The excess use of words, especially using more than are needed for clarity or precision.
parole.testo: From Middle French verbosité, from Late Latin verbōsitās. By surface analysis, verbose + -ity.

parole.significato: The greenness of lush or growing vegetation (greenery); also: the vegetation itself.
parole.testo: Inherited from Middle English verdure, from Middle French verdure, from Old French verdure, from Late Latin *viridūra, from viridis (“green”) + -ūra (abstract noun-forming suffix).

parole.significato: Standing, pointing, or moving straight up or down; parallel to the local direction of gravity; along the direction of a…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Middle French vertical, from Late Latin verticālis.

parole.significato: The state of being virulent.
parole.testo: From Middle French virulence, from Late Latin virulentia.

parole.significato: Having a thick, sticky consistency between solid and liquid (that is, a high viscosity).
parole.testo: First attested in 1605. Borrowed from Middle French visqueux and Late Latin viscōsus, from Latin viscum (“birdlime”). Doublet of viscose.

parole.significato: The condition of being visible.
parole.testo: From Middle French visibilité, from Late Latin visibilitas; equivalent to visible + -ity.
